opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most exciting ideas in the field right now, and I want to be fair to it, but I'm also a skeptic about how quickly it'll pay off. The hope comes from what we've seen with language models: you train on an enormous corpus, and all these general capabilities emerge. So the natural question is, why not do the same thing for robots? Collect a huge dataset of robot actions, train a big model, and generality falls out.

The problem is what I call the data gap. Large language models were trained on something like the equivalent of a hundred thousand years of human reading. That text was just sitting there on the internet. For robotics, we don't have anything like that. There's no internet of robot motions. Every data point has to be collected, often by a human teleoperating a robot, and that's slow and expensive. Even the most ambitious efforts so far, pooling data across many labs, amount to a tiny fraction of what the language models got. Some people say we'll close the gap with simulation, or by learning from human videos on YouTube, and those help, but each has real limitations. Simulation doesn't capture the physics of contact and friction and deformable objects very well, and videos show you what people do, not the forces and torques involved.

There's also a deeper issue. Language is already a compressed, symbolic representation. Robotics is about the messy physical world, with uncertainty in sensing, in control, and in the physical properties of objects. A tiny error in where a gripper closes can mean the difference between picking something up and knocking it over. So it's not obvious that the same scaling curves will hold.

My own view is that we shouldn't throw away good old-fashioned engineering. We have decades of work on physics, kinematics, control theory, and analytical models of grasping. I think the most promising path is to combine those with learning, using the models to get you started, then collecting data as robots are actually deployed and doing useful work. That creates a data flywheel: the robot is valuable enough to deploy, it gathers data while it works, and that data makes it better. I think that's how we'll get there, but it's going to take longer than a lot of the excitement suggests. I'd say be optimistic about the long term, but patient about the timeline.

r002.rationale: It is skeptical about the timeline, but does not address preliminary dataset successes or say that general-purpose robots are unlikely within roughly a year.

r003.rationale: It explicitly argues for combining learning with engineering approaches such as physics, kinematics, control theory, and analytical models.

r004.rationale: It attributes the data shortage to collection being slow and expensive, but does not connect the required scale to the problem’s high dimensionality.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I'd say I'm cautiously skeptical, and I want to be careful about how I say that, because I don't want to come across as a naysayer. I'm a roboticist, I've spent my whole career on this, I want robots to work. But I think there's a very seductive analogy going around right now, which is: look what happened with language models. We scaled up the data, we scaled up the compute, and these remarkable capabilities emerged. So the natural thought is, let's just do the same thing for robots. Collect enough demonstrations, enough trajectories, enough video, and out will pop a general-purpose robot.

And the problem is that the analogy breaks down in a few important places. The first is just the data itself. For language, the internet gave us trillions of tokens essentially for free, written by humans over decades. There's no equivalent for robots. There's no internet of robot motions. Every example has to be collected, usually by a person teleoperating a robot or guiding it by hand, and that's slow, it's expensive, and it's noisy. So the datasets people are excited about, which are genuinely impressive efforts, are still many orders of magnitude smaller than what a language model trains on. We're talking maybe a few million episodes versus trillions of tokens.

The second issue is the physics. Language is a closed, discrete world. You predict the next token and you're done. Robots operate in the continuous physical world, where there's friction, there's deformation, there's contact dynamics, and there's uncertainty in your sensing and your actuation. And the thing people underestimate is how sensitive manipulation is to tiny variations. If a cable is slightly stiffer, or a surface is slightly more slippery, a policy that worked beautifully in the lab can just fail. So I worry that scaling up data gives you very good interpolation within the distribution you've collected, but the real world is relentlessly out of distribution.

And then the third thing, which I say somewhat tongue in cheek, is that there's a long history in our field of people announcing that the problem is basically solved. I've been around for a few of those cycles. The grasping problem was going to be solved in the eighties, and then the nineties, and then again with deep learning. And every time we make real progress, but it turns out there's a lot more to it.

So where does that leave me? I don't think the data-driven approach is wrong. I think it's one essential ingredient. What I'd push back on is the "pure" version of the hypothesis, that data alone will get us there. I think the most promising path is what I'd call a good old-fashioned engineering approach combined with learning: you use the models and the physics and the geometry that we actually understand, you use simulation to generate data where it's cheap, and you use learning to fill in the parts that are too hard to model. And you set your expectations realistically. I'd be thrilled if in ten years we had robots that could reliably do a handful of useful tasks in homes. That would be a huge win. But a general-purpose robot that can walk into any kitchen and do whatever you ask? I think that's considerably further off than the current enthusiasm suggests, and I think it's healthy for the field to say so.

r002.rationale: It is skeptical that data alone will produce general-purpose robots soon, but does not address preliminary successes or the specific roughly one-year expectation.

r003.rationale: It explicitly argues that the promising path combines learning with engineering, including models, physics, geometry, and simulation.

r004.rationale: It says robotics data is expensive and far smaller than language-model data, but does not attribute the shortage to the problem’s high dimensionality.

astra-6.text:
I’m excited about it, but I think we have to be careful about what we mean by general-purpose. There’s a hope that if we collect enough robot data and train a sufficiently large model, we’ll get something like the leap we’ve seen in language models. That’s a compelling hypothesis. But I don’t think we yet know whether it will work that way in robotics.

One difficulty is the data itself. With language, there’s an enormous amount of text already available. With robots, collecting experience means interacting with the physical world. That takes time, things break, and data collected on one robot may not transfer straightforwardly to another robot with different sensors or a different gripper.

And then there’s reliability. A robot can do something that looks wonderful in a demonstration, but if you want it to work in your home, it has to handle all sorts of situations that weren’t in the demonstration. If it’s doing a sequence of actions, small failure probabilities can add up very quickly.

So I think large datasets are going to be important. I’m less convinced that scale alone will solve the whole problem. The question is how we combine learning with feedback, planning, and the ability to recognise when something has gone wrong and recover. I’d be very happy to see the optimistic hypothesis borne out, but I’d distinguish that hope from something we’ve already established.

r003.rationale: It says scale alone may not solve robotics and that learning must be combined with feedback, planning, and failure recovery, communicating a need for capabilities beyond training on data.

r004.rationale: It says physical-world data collection takes time, but does not attribute a data shortfall to the scale demanded by the problem’s high dimensionality.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m excited about it, but I’m skeptical of the strongest version of that claim. The hope is that we’ll see something like what happened with language models: collect enough data, train a sufficiently large model, and get a system that can generalize to tasks it hasn’t explicitly been trained to do. That’s a very interesting hypothesis. I don’t think we know yet whether it will work for robotics.

One challenge is that robot data is much harder to collect. There’s an enormous amount of text on the internet, but there isn’t a comparable supply of robots interacting with the physical world. And data collected on one robot doesn’t necessarily transfer cleanly to another, with different hands, different sensors, or a different setup.

The other issue is reliability. A robot can do something impressive in a demonstration and still fail frequently enough that you wouldn’t want to depend on it. When you’re handling physical objects, small errors can have consequences, and those errors accumulate over a long sequence of actions.

So I think large datasets will be an important part of the answer. But I’m less convinced that scaling alone gets us to a general-purpose robot. I’d want to see careful tests of how these systems perform on genuinely new tasks, how reliably they work, and whether they can recognize when they’re uncertain and recover from mistakes.
